To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the adrenocortico-steroidogenic and the hepatic naphtha-lene-metabolism responses of mallard ducks to petroleum exposure were both biphasic, with the initial response being an inhibition of adrenocorticosteroidogenesis and an increase in hepatic napolthene-metabolization, followed by a reversal of these responses after a period of time that varied with the level of petroleum exposure.

exposure of mallard ducks to crude oil for extended periods of time (1) causes a decrease in adrenocorticotropin (ACTH) secretion and (2) causes a decrease and eventual restoration in hepatic nitrification activity.

the plasma corticosterone concentrations of ducks exposed to food containing 0.5%, 1%, and 3% South Louisiana crude oil were lowered during the first 50-100 days of exposure and then increased to levels greater than normal during the subsequent 400 days of exposure.

the effects of short-term and long-term exposure to crude oil on the adrenocortico-steroid system and on hepatic mixed-function oxidase activities of mallard ducks.
the effects of petroleum on adreocortical activity in mallard ducklings and the possible relationship between the changes in adrenocorticoactivity and the changes in naphthalene metabolism.
the effect of crude oil contamination of food upon two physiological systems in mallard ducks; the adrenocortico-adrenal system and the hepatic microsomal monooxygenase system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
petroleum, when ingested in sufficient quantity, can produce both short and long term alterations in adrenocortically mediated physiological activities in mallard ducks.

acute exposure to petroleum causes an initial suppression of plasma [B] that is accompanied by an increase in hepatic nathalene-metabolism, and that the subsequent recovery of the plasma [B], which occurs in the presence of sustained elevated hepatic naphthyl metabolism, is associated with a return of plasma [B].
the acute and subacute effects of crude oil exposure on adrenocorticoid activity and on hepato-microsomal metabolism of naphthalene in mallard ducks are similar to those seen in other vertebrates.
The main takeaway from our work is that

petroleum contamination of the food of mallard ducks results in an immediate, but transient, depression of the plasma corticosterone level and in an immediate, sustained increase in the activity of hepatic microsome-mediated naphthalene metabolism.
exposure to oil, even at levels that are not considered toxic, can cause long-term effects in the adrenals.
petroleum contamination can have a profound effect on the adrenocortico-steroid axis of birds and that this effect can last well beyond the period of exposure.
